title: Savarkar portrait at Kolkata civic headquarters sparks row as Bengal asks universities to drop gowns
dek: Opposition parties accused the BJP government of rewriting Bengal's legacy; the BJP called it a manufactured controversy. Separately, the higher education department told universities to use handloom uttariyas at convocations.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
A portrait of the Hindutva ideologue V.D. Savarkar has been put up at the Kolkata Municipal Corporation (KMC) headquarters alongside seven other national figures, drawing protests from opposition parties days before the Supreme Court takes up the dispute over the city's long-delayed civic election.

The portraits were installed on the second floor of the KMC Councillors' Club, according to reports. Besides Savarkar, they include Syama Prasad Mookerjee, Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, Maharana Pratap and Rani Lakshmibai. The space earlier held pictures of deceased councillors, which have been moved elsewhere. Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari had earlier announced that Mookerjee's portrait would be installed at several places, including the KMC headquarters, and the Bharatiya Janata Party government has been installing portraits and statues of Mookerjee and other figures the party reveres.

## What each side said

Baishwanar Chatterjee, a leader of the Trinamool Congress faction led by Mamata Banerjee, said the KMC already displayed figures historically linked to the corporation, such as Deshbandhu Chittaranjan Das, Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose, Bidhan Chandra Roy and Rabindranath Tagore, and questioned why Savarkar, who he said had no connection to the civic body, had been added, according to reports.

Senior Congress leader Adhir Ranjan Chowdhury called it an attempt to "Savarkarise" the state's legacy. "Those celebrating Savarkar cannot be patriots," he said, according to reports, citing the renaming of Kolkata's port after Mookerjee.

BJP MLA and former councillor Sajal Ghosh called the opposition's stand "an unfortunate move to reap political benefits by creating unnecessary controversy". "Savarkar is directly connected to our country's freedom struggle, whether you like him or not," he said, according to reports, pointing to the years Savarkar spent in the Cellular Jail in the Andamans. He asked why critics had not objected in the past to portraits of communist figures such as Karl Marx, Lenin and Ho Chi Minh.

The KMC has had no elected board since June. The Calcutta High Court has barred the poll from being notified on the city's redrawn wards until a challenge to the new ward map is decided; the state's appeal is due before the Supreme Court on Monday, 30 November.

## Handloom instead of gowns

In a separate move, the state's higher education department has advised all state-aided universities to replace Western-style academic robes at convocations and other ceremonies with Indian attire such as the uttariya, a shawl-like stole, and garments made of handloom fabric.

In its notice of Monday to vice-chancellors, the department said the University Grants Commission had not prescribed any fixed design for ceremonial robes, leaving universities free to adopt traditional attire. It said handloom was better suited to India's climate and would support rural weavers' livelihoods. It asked universities and their affiliated colleges to "consider adopting handloom fabrics and traditional attire" and to confirm that they had received the advisory.

"We are putting effort to follow our own Indian culture and tradition. Uttariyo is enough for such ceremonies. Why do we have to wear robes?" Higher Education Minister Jagannath Chattopadhyay told reporters on Wednesday, adding that institutions including the IITs had already adopted the uttariya. He had earlier praised Jalpaiguri Government Engineering College for replacing gowns with uttariyas at its convocation.

The advisory is not binding, and no university had publicly responded to it by Thursday.
